messages.content: You design amateur rockets that fly on certified commercial motors. Work through the design, check it with the tools, and give the final design as JSON inside <design> tags. Only report results the tools returned.
Need a hand. At least 2,500 m, please. M motor or smaller. Landing speed below 6 m/s, please. Expect about 4 m/s of wind.

messages.reasoning_content:
1. Understand: Apogee at least 2,500 m (minimum). Motor class at most M (fixed ceiling). Landing speed at most 6 m/s (maximum). Wind about 4 m/s, so the flight will be run at 4 m/s. Rail length, launch angle and site altitude are not stated: I assume a vertical 1.5 m rail at sea level. Nothing asks for staging, a payload, a duration cap or a drift limit, so this is a single-stage altitude rocket with one recovery device.

2. Feasibility: A drag-free coast to 2,500 m needs burnout speed sqrt(2*9.81*2500) = 221 m/s. Drag will eat a large fraction of that, so the airframe has to stay narrow and the motor has to be a long-burn K or L rather than a short, heavy M. An M is legal but usually lives in a 75 mm case, which costs altitude. I need impulse, average thrust and loaded mass for a few 54 mm candidates before I pick one.

2. Feasibility: The K550W is a 54 mm reload with 1,620 N*s, 536 N average thrust and a 3.02 s burn. Loaded mass is 1.49 kg, of which 0.92 kg is propellant, and the only listed delay is 0 s, so I will fly it plugged and open the chute at apogee with an altimeter. The L1000W has more impulse (2,700 N*s) but the motor alone weighs 2.19 kg in the same 54 mm diameter, and the L850W is a 75 mm, 3.67 kg case. The lighter K is the one that can actually get near 2,500 m; the bigger motors mostly haul their own casing. Thrust-to-weight on a roughly 2.2 kg rocket is 536 / (2.2 * 9.81) = 24.8, far above 3, so the short rail is not the binding constraint.

3. Size: Take liftoff mass as 2.2 kg (motor plus a short phenolic airframe, fins and a small altimeter). Weight is 2.2 * 9.81 = 21.6 N, so average acceleration on the rail is (536 - 21.6) / 2.2 = 234 m/s^2 and rail exit is about sqrt(2 * 234 * 1.5) = 26.5 m/s. Burnout mass is 2.2 - 0.92 = 1.28 kg. A 5 m/s descent at Cd 0.8 needs canopy area 2 * 1.28 * 9.81 / (1.225 * 0.8 * 5^2) = 1.03 m^2, diameter sqrt(4 * 1.03 / 3.1416) = 1.15 m. I will use a 1.2 m ripstop chute so the landing sits under 6 m/s with a little margin. Coast time on a flight this high is well past any motor delay, which is why deployment is at apogee rather than on an ejection charge.

4. Draft: 62 mm phenolic tube, 0.72 m long, with a hollow polystyrene ogive and three plywood fins. The 54 mm mount is sized to the K550W case. A 30 g altimeter sits at the top of the tube. Flying it in 4 m/s wind on the assumed 1.5 m rail.

messages.reasoning_content:
4. Check: The simulator gives an apogee of 3420.6 m, which clears the 2,500 m minimum by a wide margin. Landing is 4.5 m/s against a 6 m/s maximum, rail exit is 30.5 m/s against 15 m/s, and thrust-to-weight is 26.6 against 3. The chute opens at 19.5 s, right at apogee. The flight fails the stability gate: margin at rail exit is 0.24 cal, and the minimum through the burn is the same 0.24 cal, below the 1.0 cal launch requirement. Liftoff mass came out 2.06 kg, a bit under my 2.2 kg guess, which is why the altitude is high. There is a supersonic warning (peak Mach 1.87); that does not fail a gate, but the drag model is less trustworthy up there.

5. Fix: The failing value is the 0.24 cal rail-exit margin, limit 1.0 cal. The K550W sits in the tail, so the CG is aft and the first fin set is too small to put the CP behind it. One change: four plywood fins instead of three, with root 0.22 m, tip 0.08 m and span 0.14 m. Motor, chute and tube stay as they are. Altitude has spare room above 2,500 m, so the extra fin drag is acceptable.

4. Check: The simulator gives 2449.0 m. That misses the 2,500 m minimum: 2500 - 2449 = 51 m short, about (2500 - 2449) / 2449 = 2.1%. Stability now passes, at 1.06 cal against the 1.0 cal minimum, with the same 1.06 cal as the low point during the burn. Rail exit 29.5 m/s, thrust-to-weight 25.3 and landing 4.7 m/s all clear their limits. The chute opens at 16.6 s. Still supersonic (Mach 1.5), so the drag number is the soft part of this result.

5. Fix: The failing value is apogee 2449.0 m, limit 2,500 m. The bigger fins cured the 0.24 cal margin but their drag, on a 62 mm tube, took the altitude with them. I will not shrink the fins: 1.06 cal has almost nothing to give. One change: slim the airframe from 62 mm to 58 mm with a 1 mm phenolic wall, and match the nose and the motor-mount outer diameter (0.0555 m) to that tube. Frontal area scales as (0.058 / 0.062)^2 = 0.875, about 12% less. Fins, motor and chute stay put.

messages.reasoning_content:
4. Check: Slimming the tube did not fix the altitude. The simulator gives 2447.9 m, still short of 2,500 m: 2500 - 2447.9 = 52.1 m. Stability is unchanged at 1.06 cal, rail exit 29.6 m/s, thrust-to-weight 27.4, landing 4.4 m/s. Liftoff mass fell to 1.99 kg and peak speed rose to 535.4 m/s (Mach 1.59), so the diameter cut was eaten by wave drag. The fins, not the tube, are what is holding the rocket under the target.

5. Fix: Apogee 2447.9 m is the value that still fails. I will not cut the fins, because 1.06 cal is only 0.06 cal over the gate. A faster motor would make the supersonic problem worse. I want a 54 mm long-burn with more impulse than the K550W's 1,620 N*s, or at least a slower burn that stays out of the worst drag. Looking those up before I change the design.

5. Fix: The lookups change the choice. K185W is 1,380 N*s over 7.1 s at 194 N, mass 1.43 kg, almost the same casing as the K550W. K270W has 1,970 N*s but only 245 N average, and on a roughly 2.6 kg rocket the rail estimate is (245 - 2.6 * 9.81) / 2.6 = 84.4 m/s^2, so sqrt(2 * 84.4 * 1.5) = 15.9 m/s, right on the 15 m/s gate before any wind. K700W, K1050W and the L1030 are all burned out in about 3 s, which is the same supersonic trap as the K550W. The K185W gives up (1625 - 1379) / 1625 = 15% of the impulse, and the airframe barely changes: liftoff about 1.99 - 1.49 + 1.43 = 1.93 kg, thrust-to-weight 194 / (1.93 * 9.81) = 10.2, average rail speed sqrt(2 * 90.7 * 1.5) = 16.5 m/s with (194 - 18.9) / 1.93 = 90.7 m/s^2. The 340 N spike should clear the rail, and the slower burn is what actually cuts the wave drag that a thinner tube could not. Mount length goes from 0.43 m to 0.46 m so the 0.437 m case fits. Fins stay, because 1.06 cal is the margin I am not willing to spend.

4. Check: The simulator gives 2658.4 m, so 2658.4 - 2500 = 158 m above the 2,500 m minimum. Rail exit is 19.8 m/s against 15 m/s, thrust-to-weight is 10.1 against 3, and the margin is 1.15 cal at rail exit and through the burn, against 1.0 cal. Landing is 4.4 m/s against 6 m/s, with the chute out at 18.8 s. Peak Mach is 1.04 and there is no supersonic warning this time. Motor is a K, inside the M ceiling.

5. Fix: no further change; every gate and the altitude minimum passed.

6. Uncertainty: 1.04 Mach is still transonic, so the drag model is the soft number, and 158 m of margin can disappear if the real rocket is heavier than the 1.94 kg liftoff mass. Rail exit is only 19.8 - 15 = 4.8 m/s above the gate, so a heavier build or a slower start would miss it before it missed altitude. The chute opens at 10.7 m/s, which is a hard opening for a 1.2 m canopy even though touchdown itself is 4.4 m/s. Drift is 1840 m in the 4 m/s wind because the descent from this altitude takes most of the 580.7 s flight; the prompt does not limit drift, but the field has to be large. Fin thickness and phenolic wall are on the thin side of what I would actually build.
messages.content:
K185W in a 58 mm phenolic tube, four plywood fins, and a 1.2 m chute opened at apogee.
In 4 m/s wind on a 1.5 m rail the simulator gives 2658.4 m apogee, 19.8 m/s at rail exit, 1.15 cal margin and a 4.4 m/s landing.
That clears 2,500 m, the M-class ceiling and the 6 m/s landing limit.
